title: A Simple Back from Winter Break Classroom Activity
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart lays out the lesson he uses on the first day back in January, a short thinking, writing and speaking sequence that moves students from a vague sense of their future to three written goals. He opens with a diagnosis of where the difficulty actually sits, arguing that naming big-picture aspirations is easier than mapping sub-goals, which is easier than staying on top of those sub-goals daily. He also splits student failure to build goals backward into three causes, a motivation problem from vague aspirations, a skills problem because goal-setting is not on standards lists, and a mindset problem about school being pointless. The lesson itself has two segments: a time machine free-write projected ten years into a life the student enjoys, followed by re-reading for specificity, a timed partner conversation and ten-second share-outs, then an explanation of SMART goals and six minutes to write three of them. Stuart is deliberate about the timing devices, defending the thirty-second conversation limit because students struggle to sustain an externally set conversation, and the ten-second share limit because confident volunteers overrun the floor. He models the work by writing his own goals on the board while students write theirs. The piece ends with the follow-up plan, collecting one goal per student and returning it in a month to discuss what drove success or failure. He frames the whole thing as a repeated five-things practice rather than a novel strategy.
points: Stuart's diagnostic ladder is the transferable idea: aspiration is easier than sub-goal mapping, which is easier than daily follow-through, so instruction should target the harder rungs.

The time machine prompt works because it demands specificity about relationships, work and life outside work, and is immediately followed by a re-read in which students underline concrete details or add one.
Short externally imposed time limits do real pedagogical work here, with thirty seconds forcing conversation stamina and ten seconds stopping confident volunteers from monopolising the share-out.
He teaches SMART goals with paired examples, one absurd and one academic, and writes his own goals on the board while students write theirs.

The accountability loop is what distinguishes this from a one-off new-year exercise, since students submit one goal and get it back a month later for a class discussion of what caused success or failure.
quotes: But I love the challenge of helping my students grapple with these challenges. And so even though there's a lot I want to accomplish in class during the first weeks of January, I'm going to take the time on our first day back for a simple thinking, writing, and speaking activity.

While many of my ninth grade students have at least a faint outline in their concept of “ Future Me ,” far too few consistently build goals backward from there [1]. This is partly a motivational problem — it's hard to be motivated by a vague aspiration (e.g., “I want to be a diesel mechanic because they make good money and I like trucks”) — and it's partly a skills problem — they haven't been adequately coached in goal-setting and goal-keeping (after all, those aren't on many standards lists) — and it's partly a mindset problem (e.g., “Boring things are dumb,” or “School is pointless”).

Again, I'm spending that minute walking around the class to get some formative intel on how their re-reading and revision work is going. If it turns out to be a confusing task, I re-phrase it or replace it with something else.

If you feel like 30 seconds isn't enough, try 45 or 60. The key here is that you don't want this activity to last for an entire period; I want to end class with at least a few minutes for our regular curriculum.

I'll take a handful of volunteers. Volunteer kids at this point in the year are often very comfortable speaking in front of the class; as a result, they sometimes struggle with efficient use of the floor — hence the 10 second limit.

In one month, I'll do just that. I predict that I'll find a mixed bag: some kids will have made progress, others won't. As a class, we'll spend 5-10 minutes discussing what might have caused our success or failure in keeping committed to our goals, and we'll make modifications from there.
